The patient presents with **6 months of persistent, non-fluctuating fatigue** and **unintentional 5 kg weight loss**, despite preserved appetite and absence of fever, night sweats, or constitutional symptoms typically associated with infection or malignancy. - **Highly suspicious for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)**, based on:  
  • 6-month history of fatigue + unintentional weight loss,  
  • Diffuse nontender lymphadenopathy + hepatosplenomegaly,  
  • Absolute lymphocytosis (WBC 16,000/μL) with smudge cells on peripheral smear.  
- Anemia likely due to bone marrow infiltration or autoimmune hemolysis (Coombs test pending).  
- No evidence of acute infection, endocrine dysfunction, or psychiatric cause at this time — though evaluation remains incomplete.

1. **Flow cytometry** (peripheral blood) — definitive diagnostic test.

6. **Thyroid exam and TSH** — despite low clinical suspicion.

No treatment is indicated at this time without confirmation of diagnosis and assessment of disease burden/symptoms — observation may be appropriate if asymptomatic and early-stage.

[THOUGHT]  
The clinical presentation is highly characteristic of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL): a sustained, clonal B-lymphocytosis (>5,000/μL for ≥3 months), with classic systemic symptoms (fatigue, unintentional weight loss), generalized lymphadenopathy, and organomegaly (hepatosplenomegaly). The presence of smudge cells on peripheral smear is a hallmark cytologic clue strongly associated with CLL — reflecting the fragility of neoplastic B lymphocytes during blood film preparation. The absolute lymphocytosis (WBC 16,000/μL, implying lymphocyte count well above 5,000/μL assuming typical differential) fits the diagnostic threshold. While other B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders (e.g., mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma) can present with lymphocytosis and adenopathy, they rarely show smudge cells, are less commonly associated with *diffuse* nontender lymphadenopathy + hepatosplenomegaly in an older adult, and typically lack the indolent, chronic evolution described here (6-month history). HIV must be excluded because it can cause reactive lymphocytosis and lymphadenopathy, but the absence of risk factors or opportunistic features — and the presence of smudge cells — makes CLL far more likely. Flow cytometry is definitive: CLL shows a characteristic immunophenotype (CD5+, CD23+, weak surface immunoglobulin, dim CD20, CD79b). Pending Coombs test does not rule out CLL; autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) is a well-recognized paraneoplastic complication (~10–25% of CLL cases). No evidence contradicts CLL — no fever, night sweats (B symptoms are incomplete: only fatigue + weight loss — but weight loss alone qualifies as a B symptom), no acute infection, no hypercalcemia or renal dysfunction to suggest plasma cell dyscrasia, and SPEP/immunoglobulins are pending but hypogammaglobulinemia is common in CLL.

[EVIDENCE]  
• 6-month history of fatigue and unintentional weight loss — systemic "B symptoms" consistent with CLL progression.  
• Diffuse nontender lymphadenopathy — classic physical finding in CLL.  
• Hepatosplenomegaly — indicates extranodal involvement and disease burden, common in advanced CLL.  
• Absolute lymphocytosis (WBC 16,000/μL) — meets quantitative threshold for persistent lymphocytosis required in CLL diagnosis.  
• Smudge cells on peripheral smear — highly specific morphologic feature of CLL due to fragile neoplastic B cells.  
• Anemia potentially due to bone marrow infiltration or autoimmune hemolysis — both recognized mechanisms in CLL.  
• No evidence of acute infection, endocrine dysfunction, or psychiatric cause — reduces likelihood of mimics.  
• Flow cytometry ordered as urgent next step — gold standard for confirming clonality and immunophenotype of CLL.

[GAPS]  
• Flow cytometry results — pending; required to confirm clonal B-cell population with CD5+/CD23+/dim sIg phenotype.  
• Lymphocyte count duration — summary states “6-month history” of symptoms, but does not explicitly confirm lymphocytosis has persisted ≥3 months (per IWCLL criteria); duration of lymphocytosis is unverified.  
• Peripheral blood lymphocyte morphology details beyond smudge cells — e.g., whether cells are mature-appearing, small, round, with scant cytoplasm (supportive of CLL vs. atypical or prolymphocytic morphology).  
• Bone marrow biopsy — not yet performed; though not required for diagnosis if peripheral findings are definitive, it would assess infiltration extent and cytogenetics (e.g., del(13q), del(11q), TP53).  
• FISH panel and IGHV mutation status — critical for prognostication and treatment planning, but not needed for initial diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
